newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols rise ahead of payrolls.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols rise ahead of payrolls.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options rose as bond prices tumbled and as the market prepared for Friday's November U.S. jobs data.

"Volatilities have been very low to start with," said a brokerage firm trader at Chicago Board of Trade. He said many traders seemed to be caught by surprise, but he was skeptical if there would be strong demand for volatilities beyond Friday's non-farm payroll numbers.
Implied volatility for January T-bond futures options rose nearly half a point to about 10.6 percent. March volatility was up a few tenths to 10.0 percent.
March T-bond futures tumbled nearly 1-1/2 to a low of 113-29/32 by midsession.

Brad Tyl, CBOT floor manager for Aubrey G Lanston, agreed that volatilities were not high from a historical standpoint, noting that front-month options had been above 11 percent before each monthly payroll numbers since last March.

He said the sluggishness of implied volatilities could be partly because option open interest was not concentrated near the present bond price levels. Open interest was centered on the 113 strike on the put side and 118 in calls as of Wednesday's close.
High open interest in at-the-money levels sometimes causes heavy shortcovering and option-inuduced bond price gyrations.
If March T-bonds do not fall toward 113 on Friday, implied volatilities were likely to recoil, Tyl predicted.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, an increase of 179,000 in November non-farm payrolls against a rise of 210,000 in the previous month.
Many traders expected the bonds' underlying uptrend to stay intact in the long term but said the market would be consolidative for a while.
Tyl said the high level of open interest was likely to keep weighing on the market for a while.
"This long liquidation is not over yet," he said.
Total open interest in CBOT T-bond futures rose to about 493,000 contracts Tuesday, Tyl said, noting that it had risen above 490,000 only four times in the past.
"Each time that happened, the market reversed course for a minimum of four points," Tyl said. "It just shows how frothy it got up there, just how hard the bullish sentiment was."
The shorter end of the curve was calmer due to deep-rooted expectations of a steady Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Front-end Eurodollar volatilities were flat in late trade and even softened earlier in the day.

"There's no expectation whatsoever that the Fed would do anything at the December FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting (on Dec 17)," said a Eurodollar trader at a U.S. bank affiliate. "It's very much a forgotten market at this point."

Implied volatilities for March and June Eurodollar futures options were steady at 10.5 and 14.3 percent respectively after dipping slightly earlier. Traders said a number of 1,000-lot trades took place but probably no huge high-gamma, lottery-ticket plays typical before payroll numbers.
